question: By default, is business data used to train OpenAI's models?
answers: Yes, chats help improve the models
Not by default, for business or API
Yes, unless the admin deletes the chats
Yes for the API, no for ChatGPT
fact: Business products and the API do not train on customer data by default. A customer can choose to share data, so say "by default". It is the first objection to clear.

question: What does SSO give a customer's IT team?
answers: A faster model for admin users
Automatic encryption of stored files
Permission to train on their chats
Login via their own identity provider
fact: Single sign-on lets staff log in with the company's existing login, so IT keeps one place to control access.

question: A customer's IT team asks what SCIM does. Best answer?
answers: Adds and removes users automatically
Scans prompts for personal data
Chooses which model answers a user
Encrypts the files held by the vendor
fact: It syncs with the company directory, so new joiners get access and leavers lose it automatically. IT teams love that.

question: Data residency describes where the model runs its calculations.
fact: Data residency is about where customer content is stored at rest. Where the model actually runs is a separate question, called inference residency.

question: A security team asks what zero data retention (ZDR) aims to do. Best answer?
answers: Delete a user's account on exit
Mask personal data inside prompts
Avoid keeping prompts and outputs
Block unsafe content from the model
fact: For eligible API endpoints, ZDR means prompts and outputs are not kept after processing. It needs approval and has exclusions, so get the scope in writing.

question: Who should mask personal data before an API call?
answers: OpenAI, after the call arrives
The end user, by retyping details
The customer, before data leaves
The embedding vendor, when indexing
fact: If the vendor masked it, the raw data would already have left. The customer controls what leaves the building; the provider controls what happens to it after.

question: Where do you point customers for certifications like SOC 2?
answers: The vendor's trust portal and docs
A summary that you recite from memory
The customer's own audit report
A social media post from staff
fact: Certifications are documented on the trust portal. Point customers there rather than reciting from memory, since details change.

question: A security team asks what a data processing agreement (DPA) is for. Best answer?
answers: How much the vendor charges per token
Which models the vendor will launch
Who owns the customer's brand
How the vendor may handle their data
fact: A DPA is the contract that says how the vendor may use and protect the customer's personal data. Security teams usually ask for it early.

question: A Singapore customer asks where data lives and where it runs. Best answer?
answers: Stored and run entirely in Singapore
Stored in Singapore, model runs abroad
Stored abroad, model runs in Singapore
Neither is documented or controllable
fact: For ChatGPT Enterprise, storage can be in Singapore but inference runs elsewhere. Check OpenAI's current docs before quoting, as options change.

question: A bank asks about retention controls in detail. What do you do?
answers: Reassure them it is all standard
Bring in a security specialist early
Wait until the deal is signed
Quote what you remember from a blog post
fact: Say what you know, how you would check, and bring our specialist in early, in parallel with the business evaluation. A confident wrong compliance answer loses deals.

question: A customer asks if a staff paste is a breach. What do you say?
answers: Yes, any paste is always a breach
No, vendor contracts cover everything
It depends on the model's size
That's for their own legal team
fact: Whether an event counts as a breach is a legal judgement, so we don't offer one. We can explain what is stored where, what isn't trained on, and how to delete data.

question: A customer says residency must be in Singapore. First move?
answers: Find out if it's law, policy or unease
Promise Singapore inference by year end
Offer a discount on the contract
Move on to the next objection
fact: Ask whether it is a legal clause, an internal policy or general discomfort. Discomfort is a trust problem, not a residency problem.

question: Which controls often matter more than geography?
answers: Prompt length limits and the temperature
Embedding size and chunking rules
No training by default, ZDR, encryption
Seat counts and renewal dates
fact: Be precise, not reassuring: state what is stored where, then the controls security teams weigh heavily, such as no training by default, ZDR, encryption and a DPA.

question: Some data can't leave Singapore. How could a pilot still start?
answers: Wait until every case is fully approved
Use the data anyway, then ask
Start with the non-sensitive cases
Drop the customer for now
fact: Split the use cases: land the non-sensitive ones now, and log the residency need as demand for the product team. Progress beats waiting.

question: If a hard rule needs in-country compute and we can't meet it, what then?
answers: Say so plainly and stay close
Argue that the rule is outdated
Promise to match it next quarter
Suggest they ignore the clause
fact: Staying in touch beats a promise you can't keep. The customer remembers who was straight with them when the product catches up.

question: A support bot has no source for a question. Best behaviour?
answers: Give the most plausible answer
Answer from general training anyway
Repeat the last answer it gave
Say it doesn't know and hand over
fact: Admitting 'I don't know' builds trust; a smooth guess breaks it. Good designs decline when sources are missing and route to a person.

question: A customer asks, 'When will inference be in Singapore?' Best reply?
answers: By the end of the year, I'm fairly sure
I'll log the demand; no date promised
Never; Singapore can't support it
Probably soon, a rep told me so
fact: Say 'not yet supported' and pass the demand to the product team, rather than guess a date. Don't blame Singapore's infrastructure either: that reason isn't documented.

question: Which is a typical enterprise admin control?
answers: Rewriting the vendor's privacy terms
Retention settings and audit logs
Changing the model's internal layers
Moving the vendor's servers on request
fact: Enterprise plans give admins control over retention, plus audit logs and compliance tooling. Get the current specifics from the trust pages.

question: How can a company reduce staff pasting sensitive data?
answers: One ban notice sent to staff
Turn off chat memory for everyone
Trust staff, since leaks are rare
Layers: account limits, DLP, policy
fact: Prevention is layered and never complete: block personal accounts, use admin settings, add data-loss-prevention tooling, review logs, and keep a clear acceptable-use policy.

question: Seats versus an API with a gateway: which principle holds?
answers: They differ mainly in cost
The API route is safer than seats
Each route suits different kinds of data
The API route needs fewer controls
fact: Seats suit productivity work without customer data; an API behind a gateway can handle identifiable data once it is tokenised and restored. A different class of data, not just more governance.

question: Design onboarding so the likeliest mistake becomes what?
answers: A silent error that nobody can trace
A fine paid by the vendor
A contained incident, not an open leak
An outage during the onboarding process
fact: Assume someone will paste something they shouldn't. The right contract protections and logs make that slip an incident you can contain, not a disclosure to an unvetted party.

question: What is a hard part of masking personal data first?
answers: Masked data can't be sent over HTTPS
Models refuse any masked text
Detection is never 100% accurate
Masking needs a bigger context window
fact: Personal-data detection misses things, especially varied names and nicknames, and masking can break tasks that need the real values. Treat it as one layer, with logging and review behind it.

question: How is a residency objection best reframed?
answers: Can the risk be shown to be managed?
Is the vendor's data centre big enough?
Which country has the cheapest compute?
Who wrote the cloud contract?
fact: The useful question is rarely 'is it allowed?' but 'can we evidence the risk is managed?' That moves the talk to controls, logs and review.

question: What does a data-loss-prevention (DLP) tool do?
answers: Chooses which model handles a request
Compresses long documents for storage
Rewrites prompts into plainer words
Flags sensitive data before it leaves
fact: DLP tools watch for things like account numbers or personal details leaving, and can warn or block. It is one layer alongside policy and admin settings.

question: Asked something you can't answer, what builds most trust?
answers: Give your best guess, said confidently
Be honest, then say how you'll check
Change the subject, then circle back
Promise a full answer by next month
fact: Honest limits plus a plan beat a bluff. "Here is what I know, and I'll bring in a specialist for the rest" keeps the customer's confidence.

question: Why think aloud when a customer asks something tricky?
answers: It lets them follow and correct you
It gives you time to find a script
It avoids needing to know the facts
It keeps the answer short and neat
fact: Reasoning in plain steps lets the customer follow along and spot a wrong turn early. It also shows where you would need a specialist.

question: What is an audit log for?
answers: A list of the model's training files
A cache of repeated answers
A record of who did what, to review
A backup of the prompt library
fact: Admins and compliance teams use logs to see activity, investigate incidents and show controls working.

question: Staff use personal AI accounts for work. What's the main risk?
answers: Personal accounts cost more per token
Answers get less accurate
The model refuses work topics
Work data escapes company controls
fact: There is no SSO, retention setting or admin visibility. A managed workspace with sensible policy usually beats banning tools that staff already like.

question: A security questionnaire has gaps. What's the right approach?
answers: Answer accurately and flag the gaps
Mark each line 'yes' to move fast
Leave gaps for the lawyers silently
Skip it and offer a call instead
fact: Over-claiming costs trust and can cause problems later. Honest answers with a plan or workaround keep the review moving.

question: What is data minimisation?
answers: Compressing files before upload
Sending just what the task needs
Deleting chats after a year
Using the smallest model
fact: The less sensitive data leaves the building, the smaller the risk. Mask or drop fields the model doesn't need before the call.

question: Why involve the customer's security team early in a pilot?
answers: They approve the model's prompts
A late review can stall the deal
They pick which staff get seats
They negotiate the seat price
fact: Reviews take time and have their own queue. Starting in parallel with the business evaluation keeps the deal moving instead of stopping at the end.

question: When a specialist joins the deal, what do you keep?
answers: The plan, people and timeline
Sign-off on the security answers
Drafting the legal wording
Choosing the detailed settings
fact: Specialists answer the deep questions, and you stay accountable for the plan, the stakeholders and keeping momentum.

question: Is 'never reveal customer data' in a system prompt a security boundary?
answers: Yes, models reliably obey it
Yes, if written in capitals
No, models can be talked round
Yes, at zero temperature
fact: Prompt rules guide behaviour but aren't enforcement. Real boundaries are permissions, access controls and architecture.

question: Does inference residency in a region need storage there too?
answers: No, the two settings are independent
Yes, storage there is needed first
No, inference needs no extra setup
Only for images and audio files
fact: OpenAI's help centre says in-region inference needs data residency enabled in that region first. Options change, so check the live list for the customer's country.

question: Why avoid saying 'our AI is PDPA compliant'?
answers: The law only covers paper records
Compliance is checked by the model
Compliance depends on how it's used
It sounds too cautious
fact: A product can support compliance, but the customer's configuration, data and purpose decide it. Say what controls exist and leave legal conclusions to their counsel.

question: A buyer lists three security worries. What do you do first?
answers: Answer the quickest one
Ask which one matters most to them
Promise to fix all of them
Send a link to the whole trust portal
fact: Asking shows you listen and focuses the call on what blocks the decision. Then answer each worry precisely, one at a time.

question: Why acknowledge an objection before answering it?
answers: People listen once they feel heard
It buys time to find a slide
It proves the objection is plainly wrong
It lets you skip the answer
fact: A short acknowledgement lowers defences. Then your precise answer is heard as help, not a sales push.

question: A pilot stalls at week six in security review. Likely cause?
answers: The model was too slow for the users
The pilot was too small
Security joined the pilot too late
The users were too keen
fact: Reviews take time and have their own queue. Bring the customer's security team in at scoping so it does not become a late surprise.

question: Which one is Singapore's personal data law?
answers: MAS TRM
AI Verify
SCIM
PDPA
fact: The Personal Data Protection Act governs how organisations collect, use and disclose personal data. The others are different things.

question: At recognition level, what is MAS TRM?
answers: Tech risk rules for financial firms
Personal data rules for all companies
A testing toolkit for AI models
A login standard for staff
fact: MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines set expectations for financial institutions. A bank's own teams map vendors to them.

question: At recognition level, what is AI Verify?
answers: A data residency certificate
A toolkit to test AI governance
A bank licence for AI vendors
A public leaderboard of model scores
fact: AI Verify is Singapore's AI governance testing framework and toolkit. You can name it, but leave the detail to the specialists.

question: What is IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework?
answers: A law fining unsafe AI
A cloud security certification scheme
Voluntary guidance for using AI well
A MAS rule for banks only
fact: It is voluntary guidance on responsible AI use. Customers often reference it in their own policies, so recognise it by name.

question: A bank asks, "Are you MAS TRM compliant?" Best reply?
answers: Yes, fully compliant
It does not apply to AI
That is a matter for their lawyers only
Share evidence; they map it to TRM
fact: The regulated firm owns its compliance. Offer evidence and specialists, and never claim compliance on its behalf.

question: You promised to follow up on a security point. What makes it credible?
answers: Naming who, what and by when
Following up when you remember
Sending a generic FAQ
Asking them to chase you
fact: A named owner, a clear deliverable and a date turn "I don't know" into a plan. Then keep the date.

question: Asked if customer-managed keys are supported, you are unsure. What now?
answers: Say yes, since most platforms offer it
Say no, to stay safe
Check with a specialist, then confirm
Quote last year's slide
fact: Never improvise a compliance answer. A wrong yes or no can end up in a contract or an audit file.

question: Which set is a layered guardrail design for a customer chatbot?
answers: One strong system prompt for all cases
Input checks, output checks, logging
A bigger context window
A larger model
fact: Each layer catches different failures: bad inputs, bad outputs and anything that slips through, which logs let people review.

question: Why use layered guardrails instead of one strong filter?
answers: One filter is always enough
Layers make the model faster
Regulators ban the use of single filters
Each layer catches what others miss
fact: Every control has gaps. Stacking checks, human review and logs means one miss does not become an incident.

question: A contractor left in March but still has a login in July. Likely gap?
answers: No automatic removal of leavers
No training opt-out
Weak encryption on files at rest
A short retention window
fact: SCIM syncs accounts with the company directory so leavers lose access quickly. Manual removal gets forgotten.

question: A buyer asks if their data is encrypted. Best reply?
answers: Just in transit, not at rest
Just at rest, not in transit
Yes, in transit and at rest
Ask them to check the contract
fact: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Point to the vendor trust portal for the certifications and detail, rather than reciting them from memory.

question: Why is "we have Singapore residency" an incomplete answer?
answers: It covers backups, not live chats
It may cover storage, not inference
It lapses after the first year
It applies to small files, not large
fact: Storage and model processing are separate questions. Say plainly what is stored where, and check current availability.

question: A bank hears "zero data retention". What should it ask?
answers: Which model is cheapest
Whether prompts get shorter or longer
What it covers and what it excludes
How fast replies arrive
fact: Scope depends on the product and endpoint. Ask for the written terms instead of assuming it covers everything.

question: PDPA bans sending personal data out of Singapore.
fact: Transfers are generally allowed if the recipient gives comparable protection. Some sectors have stricter rules, so check the sector.

question: Who decides if a use is allowed under their regulator?
answers: The seller
The model
The vendor's own sales and legal team
Their own compliance and legal team
fact: Sellers explain what the product does. Regulatory judgement belongs to the customer's own experts, who bear the accountability.

question: What order handles a data objection best?
answers: Reassure first, details later
Listen, diagnose, answer, confirm
Answer fast, then diagnose it later
Send documents, then wait
fact: Find out whether it is law, policy or unease, answer precisely, then check it landed. Precision builds more trust than reassurance.

question: Which control is the customer's own responsibility?
answers: Classifying their data and who sees it
OpenAI's SOC 2 audit
Encryption inside OpenAI's data centres
OpenAI's no-training default
fact: The customer controls what it sends and who can see it; the vendor controls what happens after. Classification and access rules sit with the customer.
